summary: Boarding in Seattle, through the flight, to arrival at Haneda.

attendant.kana: きゃくしつじょういん

tanaka.en: Tanaka-san, the passenger next to you

crew.kana: きゃくしつじょういん

subscenes.note: The aisle works just like a street. The direction phrases here are straight out of Lesson 4, and they all use the ～てください request form.

turns.speaker: partner
turns.en: Hello. Welcome aboard.
turns.kana: こんにちは。いらっしゃいませ。

words.anchor: a fixed greeting staff say to a customer. There is no reply to it and you never say it back. You will hear it in every shop and restaurant in Japan.

turns.speaker: partner
turns.en: What is your seat number?
turns.kana: おせきはなんばんですか。

extras.anchor: the polite お- you already use in おなまえ and おしごと
same なん as なんじ and なんですか

turns.speaker: you
turns.en: It's 25A.
turns.kana: にじゅうごのエーです。
turns.grammar: Seat numbers join the number and the letter with の. Letters of the alphabet are written in katakana: エー is A, ビー is B.

turns.speaker: partner
turns.en: This way, please.
turns.kana: こちらへどうぞ。

words.anchor: the polite member of the [[kosoado]] family. こちら, そちら and あちら are the versions you use with customers and strangers.

turns.speaker: partner
turns.en: Please go straight.
turns.kana: まっすぐいってください。
turns.grammar: いって is the [[te-form]] of いきます, and [[te-kudasai]] turns any verb into a polite request. Once you can make the て-form, you can ask for almost anything.

words.anchor: used on its own before the verb, the way you use ゆっくり in ゆっくりおねがいします

turns.speaker: partner
turns.en: Then turn left.
turns.kana: それから、ひだりにまがってください。
turns.grammar: に marks the direction you turn toward. The Lesson 4 handout writes ひだりへ; へ and に are both correct here, and に is the more common one in speech.

words.anchor: built on から, which you know as from. It strings two instructions together in order.

turns.speaker: you
turns.en: I see. Understood, thank you.
turns.kana: そうですか。わかりました。ありがとうございます。
turns.romaji: Sou desu ka. Wakarimashita. Arigatou gozaimasu.

words.anchor: the past form of わかります. Japanese uses the past here because you have just taken the information in. わかります on its own would mean I understand in general.

turns.grammar: そうですか is [[aizuchi]]: a short noise that shows you are following.

turns.stage: You reach row 25. The locker above your seat is nearly full.

turns.speaker: you
turns.en: May I put my bag here?
turns.kana: かばんをここにおいてもいいですか。
turns.romaji: Kaban o koko ni oite mo ii desu ka.
turns.source: L4 ～てもいいですか + JBP かばん
turns.grammar: [[te-mo-ii]] asks permission. It is built on the [[te-form]]: おきます becomes おいて, then もいいですか is added.

extras.anchor: the [[te-form]] of おきます. Verbs ending in く take いて.

turns.speaker: partner
turns.en: Yes, please do.
turns.kana: はい、どうぞ。

words.anchor: the same どうぞ as in こちらへどうぞ and どうぞよろしく. It offers or permits something. It never asks for something: that is ください.

turns.speaker: you
turns.en: Thank you.
turns.kana: ありがとうございます。

alternative.kana: ありがとうございました。
alternative.note: the past form, used once the thing you are thanking for is finished. See [[past-polite]].

note: This is listening practice, not speaking practice.
Real announcements are in [[keigo]], the formal register, so many of these words will be new. You are not expected to say any of it.
Read the English, then reveal it and look for the shapes you do know underneath the formal endings.
One of you can read it aloud if you want a voice in the room.
This is the announcement made once the plane is safely on its way.

turns.speaker: announce
turns.en: Everyone, thank you very much for flying with us today.
turns.kana: みなさま、ほんじつはごとうじょういただきまして、まことにありがとうございます。
turns.romaji: Minasama, honjitsu wa gotoujou itadakimashite, makoto ni arigatou gozaimasu.
turns.grammar: The standard opening of every Japanese flight announcement. Underneath the [[keigo]] it is just ありがとうございます.

extras.anchor: the formal word for きょう. Announcements and shops use it; people do not.
the word printed on your boarding pass. とうじょう is boarding; ご- is the polite prefix.
the same いただきます you say before eating. It means to receive humbly, so here the airline is humbly receiving your custom.
the formal version of とても or どうも

turns.speaker: announce
turns.en: This is Captain Yamada.
turns.kana: きちょうのやまだでございます。
turns.grammar: [role] の [name], the same [[no-linker]] as always. でございます is simply です in [[keigo]].

extras.anchor: the き is the same き as in ひこうき, airplane
です wearing a suit. Same meaning, formal register.

turns.speaker: announce
turns.en: We have just departed Seattle.
turns.kana: とうきは、ただいまシアトルをしゅっぱついたしました。
turns.romaji: Touki wa, tadaima Shiatoru o shuppatsu itashimashita.

extras.anchor: the き is the same き as in ひこうき. Announcements say とうき where you would say このひこうき.
the formal version of いま
the partner of とうちゃく, arrival. Both are written on every departure board.
しました in [[keigo]]

turns.speaker: announce
turns.en: We are scheduled to arrive at Haneda Airport at 4:00 p.m. local time.
turns.kana: はねだくうこうには、げんちじかんのごごよじにとうちゃくのよていでございます。
turns.romaji: Haneda kuukou ni wa, genchi jikan no gogo yoji ni touchaku no yotei de gozaimasu.
turns.grammar: Under the formal wrapping this is the time grammar you already have: ごご plus よじ, with に marking the clock time.

extras.anchor: くう is air, こう is port. Announcements always say the full はねだくうこう, never bare はねだ.
げんち is the local place, plus じかん, time
the same よてい as in a day's plans

turns.speaker: announce
turns.en: The flight time will be approximately ten hours.
turns.kana: ひこうじかんは、およそじゅうじかんをよていしております。
turns.romaji: Hikou jikan wa, oyoso juu-jikan o yotei shite orimasu.
turns.grammar: じゅうじかん is the duration counter you know. See [[te-imasu]]: しております is しています in [[keigo]].

extras.anchor: the formal version of ぐらい
います in [[keigo]]

turns.speaker: announce
turns.en: Drinks and a meal will be served during the flight.
turns.kana: きないでは、おのみものとおしょくじをごよういしております。
turns.romaji: Kinai de wa, onomimono to oshokuji o goyoui shite orimasu.
turns.grammar: おのみもの and おしょくじ are the same words the crew will use when the cart reaches you.

extras.anchor: き, aircraft, plus ない, inside
ようい is to prepare; ご- is the polite prefix

turns.speaker: announce
turns.en: Please sit back and enjoy the flight.
turns.kana: どうぞ、ごゆっくりおすごしください。
turns.grammar: The formal cousin of [[te-kudasai]]. ゆっくり means at your leisure, as in ゆっくりおねがいします, please say it slowly.

extras.anchor: the お～ください request shape, the formal version of ～てください

subscenes.note: This is Lesson 1 and Lesson 2 almost end to end. Put your own name and job in the blanks and say them out loud. Watch for ています: it turns up three times here.

turns.speaker: you
turns.en: Hello.
turns.kana: こんにちは。

turns.speaker: partner
turns.en: Hello.
turns.kana: こんにちは。

turns.speaker: you
turns.en: Nice to meet you. I'm ______ . I look forward to getting to know you.
turns.kana: はじめまして。わたしは ______ です。どうぞよろしくおねがいします。
turns.romaji: Hajimemashite. Watashi wa ______ desu. Douzo yoroshiku onegaishimasu.
turns.grammar: Say your own name in the blank. よろしくおねがいします has no direct English equivalent, so the English above is only an approximation. It is a fixed phrase that closes an introduction, and your handout glosses it as "Nice to meet you" or "I look forward to learning (working) with you." はじめまして covers "nice to meet you"; よろしくおねがいします is closer to "please be good to me from here on."

turns.speaker: partner
turns.en: Nice to meet you. I'm Tanaka. Likewise.
turns.kana: はじめまして。たなかです。こちらこそ、よろしくおねがいします。
turns.romaji: Hajimemashite. Tanaka desu. Kochirakoso, yoroshiku onegaishimasu.

words.anchor: こちら, this side, plus こそ for emphasis. Literally it is I who should be saying that. Use it whenever someone thanks or greets you first.

turns.speaker: partner
turns.en: Where are you from?
turns.kana: おくにはどちらですか。

words.anchor: the polite form of どこ. Same family as こちら. See [[kosoado]]. Asking おくにはどこですか is not wrong, just blunter.

alternative.kana: ごしゅっしんはどちらですか。
alternative.note: the more formal version from your handout's advanced table

turns.speaker: you
turns.en: The US. I live in Seattle.
turns.kana: アメリカです。シアトルにすんでいます。
turns.romaji: Amerika desu. Shiatoru ni sunde imasu.
turns.grammar: Living somewhere is an ongoing state rather than a one-off action, so Japanese uses すんでいます, not すみます. See [[te-imasu]]. に marks where you live.

turns.speaker: partner
turns.en: Is that so.
turns.kana: そうなんですか。

words.anchor: a warmer, more surprised version of そうですか. Both are [[aizuchi]].

turns.speaker: partner
turns.en: What do you do for work?
turns.kana: おしごとはなんですか。

words.anchor: しごと, work, with the [[polite-o]] on the front because it is the other person's job, not yours.

turns.speaker: you
turns.en: I'm an engineer at a technology company.
turns.kana: テクノロジーきぎょうでエンジニアをしています。
turns.romaji: Tekunorojii kigyou de enjinia o shite imasu.

words.anchor: English written in katakana. Sound it out and you will hear the English word.
かいしゃ from the textbook is the everyday word for company. きぎょう is the more formal one, used for larger firms.
English written in katakana. Sound it out.

turns.grammar: A long sentence, so take it in pieces. で marks where you do it: see [[de-particle]]. しています is the [[te-imasu]] form of します, which is how Japanese talks about the job you hold. If the full sentence feels like too much, エンジニアです。 on its own is a perfectly good answer, and so are がくせいです and せんせいです.

turns.speaker: partner
turns.en: Wow! That's impressive.
turns.kana: へえ～！すごいですね。

words.anchor: see [[ne-yo]]. ね invites the other person to agree with you.

turns.speaker: you
turns.en: Tanaka-san, where do you work?
turns.kana: たなかさんはどちらにおつとめですか。
turns.romaji: Tanaka-san wa dochira ni otsutome desu ka.
turns.grammar: The polite way to ask where someone works, from your handout's advanced table. おつとめ is the noun form of つとめています in the reply.

turns.speaker: partner
turns.en: I work at a bank in Tokyo.
turns.kana: とうきょうのぎんこうにつとめています。
turns.romaji: Toukyou no ginkou ni tsutomete imasu.
turns.source: L1 sample conversation + JBP ぎんこう
turns.grammar: つとめています is [[te-imasu]]: つとめます becomes つとめて, then います. に marks the organisation you belong to, and とうきょうのぎんこう uses [[no-linker]].

turns.speaker: you
turns.en: I see.
turns.kana: そうですか。

turns.speaker: partner
turns.en: Have you ever been to Japan?
turns.kana: にほんへいらっしゃったことがありますか。
turns.romaji: Nihon e irasshatta koto ga arimasu ka.
turns.grammar: This is the polite form, from the advanced question table in your handout. いらっしゃった is the honorific of いった, used about the other person, never about yourself.

alternative.kana: にほんにいったことがありますか。
alternative.romaji: Nihon ni itta koto ga arimasu ka.
alternative.note: the plainer version, also in your handout, in the basic question table

turns.speaker: you
turns.en: No, I haven't been yet. This is my first time.
turns.kana: いいえ、まだいったことがありません。はじめてです。
turns.romaji: Iie, mada itta koto ga arimasen. Hajimete desu.
turns.grammar: ～たことがあります means have ever done. Make it negative by changing あります to ありません. まだ adds not yet, which leaves the door open for the future.

words.anchor: pairs with a negative to mean not yet. Without まだ the sentence would just be a flat no.

extras.anchor: the same はじめ as in はじめまして, which literally means for the first time

turns.speaker: partner
turns.en: Really! You must be looking forward to it.
turns.kana: そうなんですか！たのしみですね。
turns.romaji: Sou nan desu ka! Tanoshimi desu ne.

words.anchor: the noun built from たのしい, fun or enjoyable. たのしみです is what you say about something still ahead of you.

subscenes.note: Lesson 3 restaurant Japanese, at 35,000 feet. Several lines here are staff-only: you will hear them constantly in Japan but never need to say them.

turns.speaker: partner
turns.en: Would you like something to drink?
turns.kana: おのみものはいかがですか。

words.anchor: the polite form of どう. どうですか and いかがですか mean the same thing; いかが is what staff use with customers.

turns.speaker: you
turns.en: Excuse me. Green tea, please.
turns.kana: すみません。おちゃをおねがいします。

turns.speaker: partner
turns.en: Yes, certainly.
turns.kana: はい、かしこまりました。

words.anchor: the very polite version of わかりました. Staff say it to customers. You will hear it often and never need to say it.

turns.speaker: partner
turns.en: Here is the meal. We have chicken and vegetarian.
turns.kana: おしょくじです。チキンとベジタリアンがあります。
turns.romaji: Oshokuji desu. Chikin to bejitarian ga arimasu.
turns.grammar: と joins two nouns as a complete list: these are the options, and there are no others.

words.anchor: English in katakana, like テクノロジー. Sound it out.

extras.anchor: the polite お- you already use in おちゃ and おなまえ

turns.speaker: partner
turns.en: What would you like for your meal?
turns.kana: おしょくじはどうなさいますか。
turns.source: L3 おのみものはどうなさいますか

words.anchor: the honorific form of します, used about the customer, never about yourself. Your Lesson 3 handout has the same phrase as おのみものはどうなさいますか. Staff-only: you will hear it and answer it, but never say it.

turns.speaker: you
turns.en: What is the vegetarian one?
turns.kana: ベジタリアンはなんですか。
turns.grammar: The most useful question shape in the language. [thing] はなんですか asks what something is, and it works for a dish, a sign, a word you did not catch.

turns.speaker: partner
turns.en: It's pasta. The chicken is popular, though.
turns.kana: パスタです。チキンがにんきですよ。
turns.romaji: Pasuta desu. Chikin ga ninki desu yo.

words.anchor: taught alongside ゆうめい, famous, in Lesson 3. にんき is about being liked; ゆうめい is about being known.
English written in katakana

turns.speaker: you
turns.en: Then the chicken, please.
turns.kana: じゃあ、チキンをおねがいします。

words.anchor: marks the moment you decide, after hearing something. It appears at exactly this point in your Lesson 3 restaurant dialogue.

turns.speaker: partner
turns.en: Certainly. Here you go.
turns.kana: かしこまりました。どうぞ。

turns.speaker: you
turns.en: Thank you. Thank you for this food.
turns.kana: ありがとうございます。いただきます。
turns.grammar: いただきます has no real English equivalent, so the English above is an approximation. It is not let's eat: it is closer to I gratefully receive this, said before the first bite whether or not anyone else is there.

words.anchor: its partner is ごちそうさまでした, said after eating. Your Lesson 3 restaurant dialogue uses both, one at each end of the meal.

turns.stage: Some time later, once the trays have been cleared away.

turns.speaker: partner
turns.en: Would you care for coffee?
turns.kana: コーヒーはいかがですか。

turns.speaker: you
turns.en: I'm fine for now. I'll have some later, thank you.
turns.kana: いまはけっこうです。あとでいただきます。ありがとうございます。
turns.romaji: Ima wa kekkou desu. Ato de itadakimasu. Arigatou gozaimasu.
turns.grammar: Straight from the けっこうです bonus box. Adding ありがとうございます is what makes a refusal sound warm rather than blunt. いただきます here means I will have it, rather than the version said before eating.

words.anchor: a polite refusal. Careful: on its own it can also mean fine, that's good, so the いま は and the tone are doing real work.

extras.anchor: the あと you met in しごとのあと, after work, in Lesson 2

alternative.kana: だいじょうぶです。ありがとうございます。
alternative.note: your handout says this is the more everyday way to decline today

turns.speaker: you
turns.en: Excuse me. A pillow, please.
turns.kana: すみません。まくらをおねがいします。

extras.anchor: no relative in class yet, but it slots into the ～をおねがいします pattern you know well

turns.speaker: partner
turns.en: Yes, one moment please.
turns.kana: はい、ちょっとまってください。
turns.source: JBP まってください／ちょっと

words.anchor: the [[te-form]] of まちます, taking the [[te-kudasai]] request shape.

note: Starts at the window, then Lesson 4 transport and Lesson 5 invitations.
Remember where you agree to meet: it matters later in the trip.

turns.stage: Mount Fuji comes into view. Tanaka-san has the window seat, so the view is past him.

turns.speaker: you
turns.en: Excuse me. May I take a picture of the window?
turns.kana: すみません。まどのしゃしんをとってもいいですか。
turns.romaji: Sumimasen. Mado no shashin o totte mo ii desu ka.
turns.source: L4 しゃしんをとってもいいですか
turns.grammar: [[te-mo-ii]] asks permission. Build the [[te-form]] first: とります becomes とって, because verbs ending in ります take って. Then add もいいですか. Ask the person whose space you are reaching across, not the crew.

extras.anchor: no relative in class yet

turns.speaker: partner
turns.en: Yes, go ahead.
turns.kana: はい、どうぞ。

turns.speaker: you
turns.en: Thank you. That's Mount Fuji, isn't it.
turns.kana: ありがとうございます。ふじさんですね。

words.anchor: in your textbook vocabulary. The さん here is mountain, not the さん you put after a person's name.

turns.speaker: partner
turns.en: That's right. It's famous, isn't it.
turns.kana: そうですよ。ゆうめいですね。
turns.romaji: Sou desu yo. Yuumei desu ne.

words.anchor: the partner of にんき, popular. ゆうめい is about being known; にんき is about being liked. Its opposite, むめい, is in your textbook too.

extras.gloss: sentence ending that tells someone something new
extras.anchor: see [[ne-yo]]. Both particles appear in this one line: よ tells, ね checks.

turns.speaker: partner
turns.en: What will you do in Japan?
turns.kana: にほんでなにをしますか。
turns.romaji: Nihon de nani o shimasu ka.
turns.grammar: This で marks where the action happens. See [[de-particle]].

turns.speaker: you
turns.en: I'd like to go to Kyoto.
turns.kana: きょうとへいきたいです。
turns.grammar: [[tai-desu]] says what you want to do. いきます becomes いきたいです.

turns.speaker: partner
turns.en: Nice! How will you go?
turns.kana: いいですね！なんでいきますか。
turns.romaji: Ii desu ne! Nan de ikimasu ka.

words.anchor: なん, what, plus the transport で. Worth knowing: in casual speech なんで can also mean why, but with a transport verb like いきます it always means by what.

turns.speaker: you
turns.en: I'll go by shinkansen.
turns.kana: しんかんせんでいきます。
turns.grammar: This で is the transport で: by train, by bus, by taxi. See [[de-particle]].

turns.speaker: partner
turns.en: I see. The shinkansen is fast.
turns.kana: そうですか。しんかんせんははやいですよ。
turns.romaji: Sou desu ka. Shinkansen wa hayai desu yo.
turns.grammar: よ tells you something you did not know. See [[ne-yo]].

words.anchor: careful, this is a second meaning. In Lesson 2 you met はやい as early, in はやいですね about waking at six. Written in kanji they are two different words; in kana they look identical, so the context tells you which one it is. A train is fast; a morning is early.

turns.speaker: you
turns.en: I want to eat Japanese food. What do you recommend?
turns.kana: わしょくをたべたいです。おすすめはなんですか。
turns.romaji: Washoku o tabetai desu. Osusume wa nan desu ka.
turns.source: L5 わしょく + L3 おすすめ
turns.grammar: [[tai-desu]] says what you want to do: たべます becomes たべたいです.

words.anchor: straight from Lesson 5, which has わしょくをたべにいきませんか. It means Japanese cuisine as a category, as opposed to ようしょく, Western food.

turns.speaker: partner
turns.en: Tsukiji is famous.
turns.kana: つきじがゆうめいです。

extras.anchor: a place name, like ろっぽんぎ and あさくさ from the textbook

turns.speaker: you
turns.en: Is that so. I'll definitely go and try it!
turns.kana: そうなんですか。ぜひ、いってみます！
turns.romaji: Sou nan desu ka. Zehi, itte mimasu!

words.anchor: your Lesson 5 expression of the day. It adds warmth and enthusiasm; はい、ぜひ！ is much friendlier than はい alone.

words.gloss: I'll go and see, I'll give it a try
words.anchor: the [[te-form]] of いきます, いって, followed by みます, meaning try doing it.

turns.speaker: partner
turns.en: Shall we grab tea together in Tokyo?
turns.kana: とうきょうでいっしょにおちゃしませんか。
turns.romaji: Toukyou de issho ni ocha shimasen ka.
turns.grammar: [[masen-ka]] is an invitation.

turns.speaker: you
turns.en: Yes, absolutely!
turns.kana: はい、ぜひ！

alternative.kana: いいですね！よろこんで。
alternative.note: also in your Lesson 5 table, slightly more formal

turns.speaker: partner
turns.en: Where shall we meet?
turns.kana: どこでまちあわせますか。

words.gloss: to meet up at an arranged place
words.anchor: starts with まち, from まちます, to wait. It means meeting somewhere you agreed on, not bumping into someone by chance.

turns.speaker: you
turns.en: How about in front of Tokyo Station?
turns.kana: とうきょうえきのまえはどうですか。
turns.romaji: Toukyou eki no mae wa dou desu ka.
turns.source: L5 + JBP とうきょうえき

words.anchor: えき, station, plus the place name. Your textbook uses とうきょうえきであいます, and Lesson 4 has しんかんせんのとうきょうえき. Name the station: Tokyo has hundreds.
position words attach with の: えきのまえ, in front of the station. See [[no-linker]].

turns.speaker: partner
turns.en: Sounds good. I'm looking forward to it.
turns.kana: いいですね。たのしみです。

title.en: Thirty minutes out: the descent announcement

note: This is listening practice, not speaking practice.
Real announcements are in [[keigo]], the formal register, so many of these words will be new. You are not expected to say any of it.
Read the English, then reveal it and look for the shapes you do know underneath the formal endings.
One of you can read it aloud if you want a voice in the room.
This is the one carrying the information you actually want: arrival time, weather and temperature on the ground.

turns.speaker: announce
turns.en: Everyone, we will shortly begin our descent.
turns.kana: みなさま、とうきはまもなくこうかをかいしいたします。
turns.romaji: Minasama, touki wa mamonaku kouka o kaishi itashimasu.

extras.anchor: the formal version of もうすぐ
the partner of りりく, takeoff
a ～します noun like べんきょう and かいもの

turns.speaker: announce
turns.en: We are about thirty minutes from Haneda Airport.
turns.kana: はねだくうこうまで、あとさんじゅっぷんほどでございます。
turns.romaji: Haneda kuukou made, ato sanjuppun hodo de gozaimasu.
turns.grammar: まで is the same as far as you use for time and distance. See [[no-linker]] for how the airport name attaches.

extras.anchor: the same あと as in あとで, later
a formal cousin of ぐらい, in the same family as およそ

turns.speaker: announce
turns.en: The current time in Tokyo is 4:00 p.m.
turns.kana: ただいまのとうきょうのじこくは、ごごよじでございます。
turns.romaji: Tadaima no Toukyou no jikoku wa, gogo yoji de gozaimasu.
turns.grammar: ごご plus よじ, exactly as taught. Note よじ, not よんじ.

extras.anchor: worth separating from じかん. じかん is a length of time, ten hours; じこく is a point on the clock, four o'clock.

turns.speaker: announce
turns.en: The weather at Haneda is clear, with a temperature of 25 degrees.
turns.kana: はねだくうこうのてんこうははれ、きおんはにじゅうごどでございます。
turns.romaji: Haneda kuukou no tenkou wa hare, kion wa nijuugo do de gozaimasu.
turns.grammar: Weather is stated as flat fact. An announcement never adds ね, because nobody can agree with a loudspeaker.

extras.anchor: the formal word for てんき, which you learned. Forecasts and announcements use てんこう.
the first of the weather set: はれ clear, くもり cloudy, あめ rain
き, air, plus おん, warmth. The ど for degrees follows the number.

turns.speaker: announce
turns.en: Please use the lavatory in good time.
turns.kana: おてあらいのごりようは、おはやめにおねがいいたします。
turns.romaji: Otearai no goriyou wa, ohayame ni onegai itashimasu.
turns.source: L4 おてあらい + real announcement
turns.grammar: おねがいいたします is おねがいします in [[keigo]]. The request underneath is one you make constantly.

words.anchor: straight from Lesson 4, おてあらいはどこですか

extras.anchor: りよう is to use, with the polite ご-. It comes back in the arrival announcement.
built on はやい, early. This is the early sense, not the fast sense.

turns.speaker: announce
turns.en: Please fasten your seatbelt.
turns.kana: シートベルトをおしめください。
turns.grammar: The formal お～ください request, the same family as [[te-kudasai]]. Probably the single most recognizable line on any Japanese flight.

extras.anchor: English in katakana. Sound it out.
しめます, to fasten, in the formal request shape

title.kana: とうちゃくのあんない

note: This is listening practice, not speaking practice.
Real announcements are in [[keigo]], the formal register, so many of these words will be new. You are not expected to say any of it.
Read the English, then reveal it and look for the shapes you do know underneath the formal endings.
One of you can read it aloud if you want a voice in the room.
Note who is speaking. The captain makes the descent announcement; this one, after touchdown, is almost always the cabin crew.

turns.speaker: announce
turns.en: Everyone, we have arrived at Haneda Airport.
turns.kana: みなさま、はねだくうこうにとうちゃくいたしました。
turns.romaji: Minasama, Haneda kuukou ni touchaku itashimashita.
turns.grammar: There is no Japanese equivalent of welcome to Tokyo. Arrival is stated as fact. The English announcement on the same flight will say welcome; the Japanese one never does.

extras.anchor: the partner of しゅっぱつ, departure. Both are on every airport board.
しました in [[keigo]]

turns.speaker: announce
turns.en: Please remain seated until the seatbelt sign goes off.
turns.kana: シートベルトのサインがきえるまで、おせきでおまちください。
turns.romaji: Shiito beruto no sain ga kieru made, oseki de omachi kudasai.
turns.grammar: まで, until, is the same まで you use for time and distance. おまちください is まってください in [[keigo]].

extras.anchor: English in katakana

extras.gloss: to go out, to switch off
extras.anchor: used of lights and signs going dark
the formal version of まってください, from まちます

turns.speaker: announce
turns.en: Please take care not to leave anything behind.
turns.kana: おわすれもののないよう、ごちゅういください。
turns.romaji: Owasuremono no nai you, gochuui kudasai.

extras.anchor: わすれ, to forget, plus もの, thing. Every station and train says this too.
the formal noun for exactly what きをつけて means in ordinary speech

turns.speaker: announce
turns.en: Thank you very much for flying with us today.
turns.kana: ほんじつはごとうじょういただきまして、まことにありがとうございました。
turns.romaji: Honjitsu wa gotoujou itadakimashite, makoto ni arigatou gozaimashita.
turns.grammar: The same sentence that opened the flight, now in the past because the flight is over. See [[past-polite]].

extras.anchor: the word on your boarding pass

turns.speaker: announce
turns.en: We look forward to serving you again.
turns.kana: またのごりようをこころよりおまちしております。
turns.romaji: Mata no goriyou o kokoro yori omachi shite orimasu.
turns.grammar: This is the airline's version of please come again. A shop says またおこしください; an airline says this. Same sentiment, different industry.

extras.anchor: the また you already use in またこんど
こころ is heart; より here means from
まちます in full [[keigo]]: humble おまちする plus おります for います

subscenes.note: The polite closing set you will reuse every time you leave someone in Japan, then your first question on Japanese soil.

turns.speaker: you
turns.en: Tanaka-san, thank you for everything.
turns.kana: たなかさん、いろいろありがとうございました。
turns.grammar: Past tense, because the conversation you are thanking him for has finished. See [[past-polite]].

extras.anchor: no relative in class yet. It gestures at all the small kindnesses at once.

turns.speaker: partner
turns.en: Likewise. Take care.
turns.kana: こちらこそ。きをつけて。

extras.anchor: no relative in class yet, but it is the standard thing to say to someone who is leaving or travelling

turns.speaker: you
turns.en: Until next time, please.
turns.kana: またこんどおねがいします。

words.anchor: you met it in こんどのどようび, this coming Saturday. こんど can mean this coming or next, and また こんど means let's do it again sometime.

turns.speaker: partner
turns.en: Yes, definitely!
turns.kana: ええ、ぜひ！

words.anchor: a softer, warmer はい. Fine in polite conversation, just less crisp.

turns.speaker: you
turns.en: I should be going now.
turns.kana: そろそろしつれいします。
turns.source: JBP そろそろしつれいします

words.anchor: your textbook gives it together with しつれいします as the set way to announce you are leaving without seeming abrupt.

turns.speaker: partner
turns.en: Thank you. Please come again.
turns.kana: ありがとうございました。またおこしください。

turns.stage: You walk up the jet bridge into the terminal and stop a member of the ground staff.

turns.speaker: you
turns.en: Excuse me. Where is immigration?
turns.kana: すみません。にゅうこくはどこですか。
turns.romaji: Sumimasen. Nyuukoku wa doko desu ka.

extras.anchor: the こく is the same word as くに, country, which you use in おくにはどちらですか

turns.speaker: partner
turns.en: Please go straight. Then turn right.
turns.kana: まっすぐいってください。それから、みぎにまがってください。
turns.romaji: Massugu itte kudasai. Sorekara, migi ni magatte kudasai.
turns.grammar: The same two instructions the attendant gave you when you boarded, with みぎ instead of ひだり. Both are [[te-kudasai]].

turns.speaker: you
turns.en: Understood. Thank you.
turns.kana: わかりました。ありがとうございます。

turns.speaker: partner
turns.en: You're welcome.
turns.kana: どういたしまして。

words.anchor: the standard reply to ありがとうございます. Long to say, but it is one fixed block, not four words.
